title: Inner products and norms
objectives: Check the inner product axioms, including covariance as an inner product on returns.

screens.title: Three ways to multiply
screens.prose: A length should come from multiplying a vector by itself. Here are three candidate products on $\mathbb{R}^2$, for $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2)$ and $\mathbf{y} = (y_1, y_2)$. Take $\mathbf{v} = (0, 1)$.
screens.question: Compute $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$ under each product.

hints.text: Both vectors are $(0, 1)$: $x_1 = y_1 = 0$ and $x_2 = y_2 = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $x_1 = y_1 = 0$ and $x_2 = y_2 = 1$ into each formula.

byKey.r1c1: With the minus sign, $0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1 = -1$. The sign stays.

explain.text: The dot product gives $1$, the true squared length. The second gives $-1$, and the third gives $0$ for a non-zero vector. Neither can be a squared length.

screens.title: Which one measures length
screens.prose: Drag $\mathbf{v}$ around the plane. The caption shows $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$ under each of the three products.
screens.question: Which product gives a positive $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$ for every non-zero $\mathbf{v}$?

options.why: Drag $\mathbf{v}$ to $(0, 1)$: it gives $-1$, and a squared length cannot be negative.
Drag $\mathbf{v}$ to $(0, 2)$: it gives 0, though $\mathbf{v}$ is not zero.
Two of them fail on the $y$-axis. Drag $\mathbf{v}$ straight up.

hints.text: At $(0, 1)$ the last two give $-1$ and 0.
Only the dot product stays positive.

feedback.correct: Right. Only the dot product is positive away from $\mathbf{0}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag $\mathbf{v}$ onto the $y$-axis and read the caption.

explain.text: $x_1^2 + x_2^2 > 0$ unless $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. $x_1^2 - x_2^2$ goes negative wherever $|x_2| > |x_1|$, and $x_1^2$ is 0 on the whole $y$-axis. A length needs both: never negative, and zero only at $\mathbf{0}$.

screens.title: The inner product axioms
screens.prose: An **inner product** on $V$ gives a number $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle \in \mathbb{F}$ for each pair. It obeys the five axioms in the table (Axler 6.2). Its **norm** is $\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}$, the $|\mathbf{v}|$ of `vectors` l3.
screens.question: Which axiom does $\langle (0, 1), (0, 1) \rangle = -1$ break, for $x_1y_1 - x_2y_2$?

options.why: Definiteness is about $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0$. This value is $-1$, below zero.
The formula is linear in $\mathbf{x}$, so sums split.
Swapping $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ gives the same real number.

hints.text: Read the first row of the table.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which row of the table does $-1$ contradict?

byKey.def: You picked definiteness, which fails at $(1, 1)$. But $-1$ is a negative value, so the axiom it breaks is positivity.

explain.text: $-1 < 0$ breaks positivity. This product also breaks definiteness, since $(1, 1)$ gives $1 - 1 = 0$. The dot product passes all five, so it is an inner product.

screens.title: A tilted inner product
screens.prose: For a symmetric $\mathbf{A}$, $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle_{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}$ is an inner product when every eigenvalue of $\mathbf{A}$ is positive (`eigen` l6). This $\mathbf{A}$ has eigenvalues 1 and 3.
screens.question: What is $\langle \mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2 \rangle_{\mathbf{A}}$?

hints.text: Row 1 times $\mathbf{e}_2$ is the entry in column 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\mathbf{e}_1^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_2$ picks out one entry of $\mathbf{A}$.

byKey.dot: You used the dot product, where $\mathbf{e}_1 \perp \mathbf{e}_2$. Here the product goes through $\mathbf{A}$.
byKey.diag: You took a diagonal entry. Row 1 and column 2 meet at the off-diagonal 1.
byKey.eig: You gave an eigenvalue. The product is one entry of $\mathbf{A}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{e}_1^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}_2 = A_{1,2} = 1$, so $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ are not orthogonal here. Also $\|\mathbf{e}_1\|_{\mathbf{A}} = \sqrt{2}$. Orthogonal and length depend on the inner product, not on the picture.

screens.title: Weighted coordinates
screens.prose: A weighted product $\sum_k w_kx_ky_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$ counts coordinate $k$ with weight $w_k$. The dot product has every $w_k = 1$. Three weight lists are on the table.
screens.question: Which weights make $\sum_k w_kx_ky_k$ an inner product?

options.why: Then $\langle \mathbf{e}_3, \mathbf{e}_3 \rangle = 0$ with $\mathbf{e}_3 \ne \mathbf{0}$: definiteness fails.
Then $\langle \mathbf{e}_3, \mathbf{e}_3 \rangle = -1$: positivity fails.
Test each on $\mathbf{e}_3$: $\langle \mathbf{e}_3, \mathbf{e}_3 \rangle = w_3$.

hints.text: A weight of 0 or below breaks an axiom on that $\mathbf{e}_k$.

feedback.correct: Right. Positive weights pass all five axioms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\langle \mathbf{e}_3, \mathbf{e}_3 \rangle = w_3$ for each list.

explain.text: $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \sum_k w_kv_k^2$, which is positive for every $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$ exactly when every $w_k > 0$. A zero weight breaks definiteness, and a negative one breaks positivity. Portfolio risk with weights on assets is built this way.

screens.title: Complex scalars need a bar
screens.prose: On $\mathbb{C}^n$ the inner product is $\langle \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{w} \rangle = \sum_k z_k\overline{w_k}$. Drop the bar and $\mathbb{C}^1$ gives $\langle i, i \rangle = i \cdot i = -1$.
screens.question: Which axiom does the product without the bar break at $z = i$?

options.why: Definiteness is about a value of 0. Here the value is $-1$.
$-1$ is real and equals its own conjugate, so symmetry holds at this pair. The trouble is the sign.
$\sum_k z_kw_k$ is linear in $\mathbf{z}$, so scalars come out of the first slot.

hints.text: Is $-1$ allowed as a squared length?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $-1$ with what positivity asks of $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$.

explain.text: Without the bar, $\langle i, i \rangle = -1$, a negative squared length. With it, $z\bar{z} = |z|^2 \ge 0$, as the second row shows. So the bar is what makes $\mathbb{C}^n$ an inner product space.

screens.title: Covariance on raw returns
screens.prose: On return vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$, set $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle = \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \tfrac1n \sum_k (x_k - \bar{x})(y_k - \bar{y})$, as in `eigen` l7. A cash account returns 0.01 every day.
screens.question: Which axiom fails for covariance on raw returns?

options.text: Positivity: a variance can be negative
options.why: A variance is a mean of squares, so it is never negative.
$\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z}) = \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}) + \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{z})$ does hold.

options.text: None: covariance is an inner product on all returns
options.why: Cash has variance 0 and is not the zero vector. One axiom fails.

hints.text: Zero variance on a non-zero vector breaks definiteness.

feedback.correct: Right. Cash has zero variance without being zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\langle \text{cash}, \text{cash} \rangle$ from the table.

byKey.pos: You picked positivity, but a variance is never negative. The failure is a zero variance on a non-zero vector.

explain.text: Cash is not $\mathbf{0}$, yet $\mathrm{Var}(\text{cash}) = 0$, so definiteness fails. Demeaning sends cash to $\mathbf{0}$. On the subspace of zero-mean vectors (l2) covariance is an inner product, and $\|\mathbf{x}\|$ is the standard deviation.

screens.title: Norms scale
screens.prose: Every inner product gives a norm $\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}$. We met four: dot, weighted, $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}$ and $\sum_k z_k\overline{w_k}$. Covariance on zero-mean returns is a fifth, and the quiz adds $\int_0^1 fg$. Scaling a vector scales its norm: $$\|\lambda\mathbf{v}\| = |\lambda|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|.$$
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: $\|\lambda\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \langle \lambda\mathbf{v}, \lambda\mathbf{v} \rangle$, by the definition of the norm.
$= \lambda\langle \mathbf{v}, \lambda\mathbf{v} \rangle$, by homogeneity in the first slot.

lines.why: In the second slot $\lambda$ comes out as $\bar{\lambda}$. With $\lambda = i$, $\lambda^2 = -1$ would make a norm negative.

hints.text: Out of the second slot a scalar comes as its conjugate.

feedback.correct: Right. The second slot gives $\bar{\lambda}$, and $\lambda\bar{\lambda} = |\lambda|^2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take $\lambda$ out of the first slot, then out of the second.

byKey.x1: You took $\lambda$ out of the second slot unchanged. There it comes out conjugated, as $\bar{\lambda}$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Homogeneity takes $\lambda$ out of the first slot, and conjugate symmetry takes $\bar{\lambda}$ out of the second. So $\|\lambda\mathbf{v}\|^2 = |\lambda|^2\|\mathbf{v}\|^2$. Over $\mathbb{R}$ the bar does nothing, and $\|{-2}\mathbf{v}\| = 2\|\mathbf{v}\|$.

screens.title: Pythagoras proved
screens.prose: Call $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ **orthogonal** when $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0$. Prove Pythagoras (Axler 6.12) from the axioms alone.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: $\|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\|^2 = \langle \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \rangle$, by the definition of the norm.
$\|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\| = \|\mathbf{u}\| + \|\mathbf{v}\|$, since the sides meet at a right angle.
lines.why: Sides 3 and 4 give a hypotenuse of 5, not 7. Pythagoras adds squares.

hints.text: Write the squared norm as an inner product.
Expand it into four terms by additivity.
The two cross terms are $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$ and its conjugate, both 0.

feedback.correct: Right. The two cross terms are 0, so the squares add.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand $\langle \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \rangle$ into four terms.

byKey.x1: You added the lengths. Pythagoras adds the squared lengths: 3 and 4 make 5.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Expanding gives four terms, and the two cross terms are $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$ and its conjugate. Both are 0, so $\|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{u}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2$. The proof works in every inner product space, functions and returns included.

screens.title: A norm with no inner product
screens.prose: Expand both squares as in the last proof: the cross terms cancel. So every inner-product norm obeys $\|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|^2 = 2(\|\mathbf{u}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2)$. Test the max norm $\|(a, b)\|_\infty = \max(|a|, |b|)$ on $\mathbf{u} = (1, 0)$, $\mathbf{v} = (0, 1)$.
screens.question: What is $\|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\|_\infty^2 + \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|_\infty^2$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the larger absolute entry of $(1, 1)$ and of $(1, -1)$, then square and add.

byKey.four: You used the Euclidean norm, or the right side. In the max norm $\|(1, 1)\|_\infty = 1$.
byKey.one: You found one square. Add $\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|_\infty^2 = 1$ as well.

explain.text: $\max(1, 1) = 1$ for both, so the left side is $1 + 1 = 2$, but the right side is $2(1 + 1) = 4$. The law fails, so no inner product has the max norm as its norm. Some norms, like this one, come from no inner product.

screens.title: Adding two uncorrelated books
screens.prose: Two strategies have daily P&L standard deviations of £3k and £4k, and they are uncorrelated. In the covariance inner product on demeaned P&L, uncorrelated means orthogonal, and the norm is the standard deviation.
screens.question: What is the standard deviation of the combined daily P&L?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use Pythagoras on the norms 3 and 4, in £k.

byKey.add: You added the standard deviations. Orthogonal norms add in squares: $\sqrt{9 + 16}$.
byKey.diff: You subtracted. Uncorrelated risks never cancel; their squares add.

explain.text: Orthogonal P&L vectors obey Pythagoras: $\sigma^2 = 3^2 + 4^2 = 25$, so $\sigma = 5$, which is £5k and not £7k. That is why uncorrelated books diversify. The correlated case needs the cross term, in l12.

ideas: An inner product obeys positivity, definiteness, additivity and homogeneity in the first slot, and conjugate symmetry. Its norm is $\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}$.
Examples: the dot product, positive weights, $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{y}$ with positive eigenvalues, $\int_0^1 fg$ on continuous functions, $\sum_k z_k\overline{w_k}$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$.
Covariance is an inner product on zero-mean returns, with the standard deviation as norm. Orthogonal means uncorrelated, and Pythagoras adds variances.
summary.trap: Covariance on raw returns is not an inner product: cash has variance 0 but is not $\mathbf{0}$. Definiteness fails, not positivity.

quiz.prose: In the proof of Pythagoras, $\|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\|^2$ expands to $\|\mathbf{u}\|^2 + \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle + \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u} \rangle + \|\mathbf{v}\|^2$.
quiz.question: Why do the two middle terms vanish when $\mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v}$?

options.text: They are negatives of each other, so they cancel
options.why: They are conjugates, not negatives. Each is 0 on its own.
Neither norm need be 0: $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ are orthogonal.
Positivity is about $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$. These are cross terms.

feedback.correct: Right. Orthogonality kills one, and conjugate symmetry the other.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$ for orthogonal vectors?

explain.text: Orthogonal means $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0$. Conjugate symmetry gives $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u} \rangle = \bar{0} = 0$. Only the two squares are left.

options.why: $x_1^2 \ge 0$ for every vector, so positivity holds.
$x_1y_1$ is linear in $\mathbf{x}$, so sums split.
$(0, 1) \ne \mathbf{0}$ has $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0$, which one axiom forbids.

feedback.correct: Right. A non-zero vector with $\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0$ breaks definiteness.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Is $(0, 1)$ the zero vector?

explain.text: $\langle (0, 1), (0, 1) \rangle = 0$, though $(0, 1) \ne \mathbf{0}$. Definiteness says only $\mathbf{0}$ may give 0. Positivity holds, since $x_1^2 \ge 0$.

quiz.prose: Let $f$ on $[0, 1]$ be 0 except $f(\tfrac12) = 1$. Then $\int_0^1 f^2 = 0$, though $f$ is not the zero function (`analysis` l15-epsilon-delta treats continuity).
quiz.question: Why is $\langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^1 fg$ defined only on continuous functions?

options.text: On all functions definiteness fails; a continuous $f$ with $\int_0^1 f^2 = 0$ must be 0

options.why: $f^2 \ge 0$, so $\int_0^1 f^2 \ge 0$ for any integrable $f$.

options.text: Only continuous functions can be multiplied
options.why: Any two functions multiply. The issue is a non-zero $f$ with $\int_0^1 f^2 = 0$.
$\int_0^1 fg = \int_0^1 gf$ for any integrable $f$ and $g$.

feedback.correct: Right. Continuity rules out a lone spike.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which axiom does the spike $f$ break?

explain.text: The spike $f$ is non-zero, yet $\int_0^1 f^2 = 0$, so definiteness fails on all functions. A continuous $f$ with $f(c) \ne 0$ stays away from 0 near $c$, so $\int_0^1 f^2 > 0$. So the integral product is an inner product on continuous functions.

quiz.prose: On continuous functions on $[0, 1]$, take $\langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^1 f(x)g(x)\,dx$.
quiz.question: What is $\langle 1, x \rangle$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $1 \cdot x$ from 0 to 1.

explain.text: $\langle 1, x \rangle = \int_0^1 x\,dx = \tfrac12$. So 1 and $x$ are not orthogonal on $[0, 1]$. On $[-1, 1]$ they are, which l13 uses.
